title: Jacob Goes Down to Egypt
summary: Jacob sets out for Egypt and stops at Beersheba to offer sacrifices, where God speaks to him in a night vision, telling him not to fear, promising to make him a great nation in Egypt, to go down with him, and to bring him back. The chapter lists the seventy members of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt. Jacob and Joseph are reunited in Goshen, and Joseph coaches his family on how to present themselves to Pharaoh as herdsmen.
story: Jacob's decision at the end of Genesis 45 was made in joy, but leaving the promised land was no small thing. Abraham's trip to Egypt had ended badly (12:10-20), and God had told Isaac not to go down there at all (26:2). God had also told Abraham that his descendants would be strangers in a land not their own, oppressed for four hundred years, and then brought out with great possessions (15:13-14). This chapter is the moment that word begins to come true. God meets Jacob at the border of the land and gives him the promise he needs: Egypt will not end the story but become the place where the family grows into a nation. These are the last words God speaks in Genesis. The list of names that follows is the family God will make into Israel, and the book of Exodus opens by repeating it.
historical:
Beersheba lay at the southern edge of Canaan, on the road toward Egypt, and was a place of worship in the family's memory. Abraham had planted a tree and called on the name of the LORD there (21:33), and God had appeared to Isaac there with the words “Do not be afraid, for I am with you” (26:24). Jacob stops at the same place before leaving the land.

The movement of herding families from Canaan into the eastern Nile Delta is well attested. A wall painting in the tomb of Khnumhotep II at Beni Hasan, from around 1890 BC, shows a group of Asiatic men, women, and children in colorful garments arriving in Egypt with their donkeys. A much later Egyptian document, Papyrus Anastasi VI from the late thirteenth century BC, records a frontier official allowing herders from Edom to pass the border fortress to reach the pools of Pithom and keep themselves and their flocks alive. Jacob's family belongs to that kind of movement: a clan of herders seeking food and pasture in the Delta during a famine.
cultural:
The list counts “persons” (the Hebrew nephesh), and like most ancient genealogies it is organized by fathers and sons. Only two women are named among the descendants, Jacob's daughter Dinah and Asher's daughter Serah, and the wives of Jacob's sons are expressly left out of the count (v. 26). One of Simeon's sons is identified as the son of a Canaanite woman (v. 10), a note that the family had already begun marrying into the land.

God's promise that Joseph's own hands would close Jacob's eyes (v. 4) refers to the custom of a close relative closing the eyes of the dead. For a man who had mourned Joseph as dead for more than twenty years, it was a promise of a good death with his son beside him. Joseph's advice at the end of the chapter reflects Egyptian social attitudes. The narrator says all shepherds were detestable to the Egyptians, a settled farming people, and by presenting themselves honestly as herdsmen the family would be given land apart, in Goshen. Separation that looked like a social slight would help keep Israel a distinct people.
literary: The chapter has four parts: the vision at Beersheba, the list of names, the reunion, and the plan for meeting Pharaoh. God's call, “Jacob, Jacob!”, and Jacob's reply, “Here I am”, follow the same pattern as God's call to Abraham at Moriah (22:11) and to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:4). The genealogy is arranged by Jacob's four wives, with Leah's descendants numbering thirty-three, Zilpah's sixteen, Rachel's fourteen, and Bilhah's seven; each maid's line is about half that of her mistress. The total of seventy (v. 27) is a number of fullness, and it matches the seventy nations listed in the Hebrew text of Genesis 10, as if the family of promise were a small counterpart to the whole world it was meant to bless. The chapter's emotional peak is brief: Joseph falls on his father's neck and weeps, and Jacob says, “Finally I can die, now that I have seen your face and know that you are still alive!”

outline.t: God's word to Jacob at Beersheba and the move to Egypt
The descendants of Bilhah and the total of seventy
Jacob and Joseph reunited in Goshen
Joseph prepares the family to meet Pharaoh

doctrines.note: God renews his promise to Abraham's family at the point of leaving the land: “I will make you into a great nation there.” The promise of a great nation (12:2) will be fulfilled not in Canaan but in Egypt, the very place that will later enslave them. God's covenant faithfulness works through unexpected places.

God does not only permit the move; he directs it and goes with it. The famine, Joseph's rise, and Pharaoh's wagons all serve a plan God announced generations earlier (15:13-14), and the chapter shows God speaking to confirm that the road runs through his will.

“I will surely bring you back” (v. 4) is a promise Jacob will not see fulfilled in his lifetime, except in the return of his body for burial (Genesis 50). The promise points beyond him to the exodus, and it teaches his descendants to live in Egypt as people whose future lies elsewhere.

words.note: Yarad, to go down. Travel from Canaan to Egypt is always going down in Hebrew, both geographically and, in Genesis, often ominously. God tells Jacob not to be afraid to go down to Egypt and then promises, “I will go down with you to Egypt” (v. 4). In Exodus 3:8 the same verb describes God coming down to rescue his people from Egypt.

Goy, nation. God promises to make Jacob into a great nation in Egypt (v. 3), repeating the first promise to Abraham (12:2). The word usually refers to a people as a political and ethnic body, and elsewhere often to the non-Israelite nations. The family of seventy is to become a people, a transformation the opening verses of Exodus report.

Shiv'im, seventy. The total of Jacob's family (v. 27) is repeated in Exodus 1:5 and Deuteronomy 10:22. Seventy is a round number of completeness in the Bible, and the count here is arranged to reach it, including Jacob, Joseph, and Joseph's sons. How the numbers relate to the seventy-five of Acts 7:14 is taken up in the hard question.

christ: God's promise, “I will go down with you to Egypt,” is the heart of this chapter and a thread that runs to Christ. The God who goes down with his people into a foreign land is the God who, in the fullness of time, came down to be with his people in the person of Jesus, called Immanuel, God with us (Matthew 1:23). Matthew also sees the pattern of this chapter repeated in Jesus' own life. The child Jesus is taken down to Egypt to escape a murderous king, and Matthew applies to his return the words of Hosea 11:1, which first referred to Israel: out of Egypt God called his son (Matthew 2:15). The list itself contains Perez and Hezron (v. 12), names that appear in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:3). The chapter does not predict Christ, but it shows the shape of his story: the son who goes down into Egypt and is brought up again.

hard.q: Genesis says seventy went down to Egypt, but Stephen says seventy-five (Acts 7:14). Which is right?
hard.a:
The two numbers come from different forms of the Old Testament text. The Hebrew text of Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5 reads seventy. The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament made in the last centuries BC, widely used by Greek-speaking Jews and early Christians) reads seventy-five in both places, apparently counting additional descendants of Joseph's sons, and a Hebrew manuscript of Exodus from among the Dead Sea Scrolls also reads seventy-five in Exodus 1:5. Stephen, speaking in a Greek-speaking setting, follows that form of the text. Neither number is a head count of everyone who traveled, since wives and servants are not included.

The counting within Genesis 46 also takes some care. Verse 26 gives sixty-six, which excludes Jacob himself, Joseph, and Joseph's two sons (already in Egypt). Verse 27 reaches seventy by adding them back, and the thirty-three of Leah's line in verse 15 appears to include Jacob. Readers explain these differences as different ways of reckoning the same family rather than contradictions; the lists aim to show a complete family, not to supply a census.

questions: Jacob stops to worship before leaving the land, and God tells him not to be afraid. What fears do you carry into a major change, and what would it mean to hear “I will go down with you” in that place?
Most of the people in this list are only names. Why might it matter that Scripture records the ordinary members of a family, not only its heroes?
Joseph told his family to be honest about being herdsmen even though it lowered their status in Egypt. When has honesty about who you are cost you standing but protected something more important?
